entry.title: Gen V
entry.content:
Season 1

I watched Season 1 of Gen V while rowing, as I watch most TV, and I really enjoyed it. It felt reminiscent of Buffy the Vampire Slayer in that we had a cast of characters, all of which are interesting, romantically in motion, and of course set in a school environment.

There wasn't anything in particular I can remember a few months later that I liked about Season 1, but i feel like the characters were compelling, the visual effects were good, and I appreciated that it felt like The Boys but with more local stakes instead of the end of the world.

Season 2

Season 2 of Gen V is an interesting case-study in what happens when one of your main actors passes away right before shooting. While the show does recover, it is very apparent something is off because of both how the character is written off, and the vibe of the actors on screen at the start of the season.

The character dies off screen and in the past something that never happens in any The Boys/Gen V show before or after. Unlike every other death, which is a big show with a bunch of build-up, this just... happened as the season began. It's a shock to everybody involved, and the show does a good enough job of honoring Chance Perdomo any way they can. He was a great actor, I really liked his work, and I do think the show would have been 1000x better with him around.

Ironically a character dying suddenly and off screen everybody else finding out about it randomly would be very original storytelling -- that's how people die in real life and it's something that most media gets wrong. People don't die in a big explosion... they trip and fall down the stairs, or get in a car accident, or die in their sleep.

The season takes a few episodes to emotionally recover from the shock of Chance's passing, and eventually I think does find it's footing and I think has a solid finish.

I believe this is the end of Gen V so I feel comfortable reflecting on the show in general.

While Gen V has good special effects, I would say at it's best Gen V is on par with The Boys, it suffers more from the tension in most prestige television shows which is that it both has to feel fresh and original, like a movie, but has to fill in ~6-8 hours of screen time, like TV, and it starts to feel stale by the end.

The finale is fun and exciting, but there are episodes here and there where it feels like we're spiraling, going nowhere over and over, and while sometimes characters change, they ultimately feel like they come back to the original state without having really accomplished any growth.

If Gen V were to lean into being more of a Buffy show, with a Monster of the Week (or Supe of the Week) formula, I think it would have done great, but with 8 episode seasons it's really got to focus on the main plot in a way that those shows can breathe a bit more.

Is Gen V great TV? No, but it is a totally solid exciting super-hero drama you can put on while rowing.

entry.title: What If...? (2021 - 2024)
entry.content:
I watched Seasons 2 and 3 of What If while rowing this month. It's a super silly show with very low stakes and a pretty good and consistent pace, making it easy to row to.

I do wish it kept going after season 3. I could basically watch this show forever, in the same way I can watch content like TikTok forever. It scratches an itch, it's fun to watch, but honeslty I couldn't tell you what happened in any of the episodes...

entry.title: Pluribus (2025)
entry.content:
During some travel in early January I downloaded and watched Pluribus knowing very little about the show, just that it was made by Vince Gilligan which is enough to get me on board.

I really enjoyed the deep dive into what it would be like to "live with a hive mind".

I also really enjoyed the tact that the story had in it's critique of LLMs, although I think those critiques go beyond LLMs which I appreciate.

Once scene in which a culture is erased in a very clinical fashion was really interesting and brilliant writing.

The show is written in such a way that a lot of it can be seen as critiques of modern problems, like LLMs, but "in the fiction" enough that in 10 or 20 years I think it'll be worth re-watching as those same devices will likely feel like comments on new modern problems. Good writing. Good story telling.

entry.title: The Boys (2019-2026)
entry.content:
Season 3 (2022)

I really like the show (so far). The visuals are insane, the characters get themselves into crazy shit that is unlike anything I've seen on screen before. My only gripe is that main characters have a hard time dying so I never worry about the consequences for what's happening. Sitcom logic is a-ok, but it makes the evolving story feel more stagnant that I would have liked.

Solder-boy the stand-in for "classic patriotism" in contrast with modern (Homelander) patriotism works well.

Homelander not only surviving but coming out somehow better after all the heinous shit he does this season is a great Trump allegory and honestly I am really dreading (in a good way) the stuff he's going to get away with the next two seasons.

I was supposed to talk about Season 4 of The Boys but It's been a few months since I watched that and I have since completely forgotten anything to do with that particular season... oops!

Season 5 (2026)

This season got a lot of flack, at least on Reddit, and I cannot for the life of me tell you why.

Was Season 5 of The Boys brilliant? No.

Was Season 5 of The Boys consistent with Seasons 2, 3, and 4? Yes!

Here's a bullet list of my thoughts about the season in no particular order:

  • The concentration camps kept coming up, but ultimately were resolved too easily.
  • The Gen V tie-in was really disappointing and did not feel like pay-off for watching 2 seasons of another show.
  • The finale was satisfying, but not nearly badass (or wimpy, choose one extreme) for the build-up.
  • I like that pretty much all the shitty bad guys died and all the good guys (with some exceptions) lived happily ever after.

I need to think of a word for this, but The Boys also suffered from the problem of a prestige show being awesome in it's first season, and then it can either continue to innovate, and risk alienating it's audience, or stay consistent with it's first season, and risk getting stale. I think The Boys walks the line pretty well but ultimately falls on the consistent side of the spectrum which ends up making the last season feel meh when in my opinion it's as good as the beginning of the show, we've just been watching that show for like... 40 episodes.
